items.title: Assist (official scoring judgement)
items.summary: An assist is credited to the player whose pass leads directly to a teammate's made field goal, as judged by the official scorer.

items.title: Away-from-the-play foul
items.summary: A deliberate defensive foul away from the ball in the last two minutes, or before a throw-in is released, gives one free throw and possession.

items.title: Blocked shot
items.summary: A block is credited to a defender who legally deflects a field goal attempt and prevents it from scoring.

items.title: Clear-path foul
items.summary: A clear-path foul is a defensive foul that takes away a transition scoring chance with no defender ahead; it brings two free throws and the ball.

items.title: Coach's challenge
items.summary: A head coach may challenge certain calls once per game, using a timeout; a successful first challenge earns a second.

items.title: Flagrant fouls
items.summary: A flagrant foul is unnecessary contact (penalty 1) or unnecessary and excessive contact (penalty 2); both give two free throws and the ball.

items.title: Free throws
items.summary: A free throw is an unguarded one-point attempt from the foul line, awarded mainly for shooting fouls and penalty fouls.

items.title: Game structure and regulation time
items.summary: An NBA game is four 12-minute periods; a tie after the fourth period is settled by overtime.

items.title: Garbage time (analytical term)
items.summary: Garbage time is the informal name for late minutes in a decided game, when regular players sit and the play is unrepresentative.

items.title: Instant replay review
items.summary: Officials and the league's replay centre review defined categories of plays, such as shot value, end-of-period shots and flagrant fouls.

items.title: Jump balls and opening possession
items.summary: The NBA starts the game and each overtime with a jump ball and uses jump balls, not an alternating arrow, for held balls.

items.title: Offensive and defensive rebounds
items.summary: A rebound is credited for gaining the ball after a missed shot: offensive if the shooting team recovers it, defensive if the other team does.

items.title: Official scoring and stat corrections
items.summary: Box-score statistics are recorded by scorers in real time and can be corrected after the game.

items.title: Overtime
items.summary: A tied NBA game continues with five-minute overtime periods until one team leads at the end of a period.

items.title: Personal fouls and disqualification
items.summary: A personal foul is illegal contact with an opponent; a player's sixth personal foul in an NBA game disqualifies him.

items.title: Possession
items.summary: A possession is one team's continuous period of control of the ball, ending when the other team gains it or a score or period ends it.

items.title: Scoring values: two, three and one
items.summary: A field goal is worth two or three points depending on where the shooter stands; a free throw is worth one.

items.title: Steal
items.summary: A steal is credited to a defender who takes the ball from an opponent, intercepts a pass or deflects it so that his team gains possession.

items.title: Substitutions
items.summary: Substitutes report to the scorer and enter during a dead ball when an official beckons them; there is no limit on the number of substitutions.

items.title: Team fouls and the penalty (bonus)
items.summary: From a team's fifth foul in a regulation period, each common foul sends the opponent to the line for two free throws.

items.title: Technical fouls
items.summary: A technical foul penalises unsportsmanlike conduct or certain procedural violations with one free throw; two unsportsmanlike technicals bring ejection.

items.title: The 14-second reset
items.summary: After an offensive rebound, and in some frontcourt stoppages, the shot clock is set to 14 seconds instead of 24.

items.title: The 24-second shot clock
items.summary: A team must release a shot that touches the rim within 24 seconds of gaining possession.

items.title: Timeouts
items.summary: Each NBA team has seven timeouts in regulation, with limits late in the fourth period, and two per overtime.

true-shooting-percentage.title: True shooting percentage (TS%)
true-shooting-percentage.summary: Points scored per two scoring attempts, where attempts include field goals and an allowance for free throws.

sources.title: Basketball-Reference.com Glossary
sources.note: TS% = PTS / (2 * TSA), TSA = FGA + 0.44 * FTA; opened 2026-11-26

true-shooting-percentage.body: True shooting percentage measures scoring efficiency across all three ways of scoring. The denominator, true shooting attempts, is field goal attempts plus 0.44 times free throw attempts; the coefficient is below one half because some free throws - and-ones, technicals, three-shot fouls - do not use up a separate possession. Points are divided by twice that number, so the result reads like a shooting percentage: a player who scored exactly two points per attempt would be at 100 percent. Unlike field goal percentage it gives full credit for the third point on a three and for points at the line, which makes it the fairest single comparison between, say, a three-point shooter, a mid-range scorer and a player who lives at the foul line. It should always be read with volume and role in mind, because efficiency is easier to sustain on few, selective attempts. All its inputs - points, field goal attempts and free throw attempts - are in our historical box scores.
data_gaps: no shot locations or shot difficulty
limitations: The 0.44 coefficient is a league-wide approximation; the true share varies by player and season.
Unstable on small numbers of attempts.
evaluation_questions: A player scores 24 points on 15 FGA and 6 FTA. What is his TS%?
Why is the free throw coefficient less than 0.5?

drop-coverage.title: Drop coverage
drop-coverage.summary: Against a pick-and-roll the screener's defender retreats toward the paint while the on-ball defender chases over the screen.

sources.title: FIBA World Association of Basketball Coaches documents
sources.note: federation coaching manuals cover this topic; pointer only, the manuals were not opened for this record

drop-coverage.body: Drop coverage is the conservative answer to the pick-and-roll. The big defender backs away from the screen and positions himself between the ball and the rim, deep enough to stop a layup and to stay in contact with the roller. The guard fights over the top of the screen and pursues from behind. The scheme keeps two defenders on the two attackers, so the other three can stay with shooters and no rotation is required. It protects the rim and the three-point line at once and concedes the space between them: the pull-up jumper and the floater. Against handlers who shoot well off the dribble, or screeners who pop to the arc, that concession becomes expensive. Drop coverage keeps big men out of long recoveries and away from the perimeter, which suits slow-footed rim protectors and helps defensive rebounding. In general terms it tends to leave the ball handler to score while holding down the assists that come from help rotations.
limitations: General description; our data cannot confirm which scheme any team uses in a given game.
The statistical tendency described is a general expectation, not a measured relationship in our data.
Teams mix coverages within a game.
drop-coverage.common_responses: Pull-up jumpers and floaters, pick-and-pop with a shooting big, Spain action to screen the dropping big, and re-screening to give the handler a second advantage.
evaluation_questions: Which shots does drop coverage concede by design?
Why does drop coverage require no rotation from the other three defenders?
drop-coverage.player_responsibilities: Big defender: retreat to the level that stops both the layup and the lob, stay between ball and rim. Guard: fight over the screen and chase to contest from behind. Others: stay attached to shooters.

usage-percentage.title: Usage percentage (USG%)
usage-percentage.summary: An estimate of the share of team plays a player used while he was on the floor.

sources.title: NBA Stats Glossary
sources.note: USG% defined as (FGA + possession-ending FTA + TO) / POSS; opened 2026-11-26

usage-percentage.body: Usage percentage counts the plays a player ends - field goal attempts, free throw trips and turnovers - and divides by the plays his team ended during his minutes. The widely used box-score form scales the team's totals by the fraction of team minutes the player was on court, since the box score does not say what happened while he played. Free throw attempts are multiplied by 0.44 to approximate the number of possessions they consumed. The league's own statistics site defines the same idea with counted possessions: field goal attempts, possession-ending free throw attempts and turnovers over possessions played. The two versions agree closely for regular players and can differ in short minutes. An even share among five players is 20 percent. Usage describes how much of the offence a player finishes; it does not include passes, so creators who set up others are understated, and it says nothing about efficiency. In our data the figure is supplied by the provider and its exact method has not been verified.

related.title: Usage as a measure of opportunity

data_gaps: no counted on-court team possessions for historical games
limitations: The 0.44 coefficient is an approximation and other values are sometimes used.
Box-score and possession-counted versions differ, especially in small samples.
Excludes assists and passing; not a measure of ball dominance or quality.
evaluation_questions: What is each player's usage if five teammates share plays equally?
A player has 18 FGA, 8 FTA and 3 TOV in 36 of his team's 240 minutes; the team has 88 FGA, 25 FTA and 14 TOV. Estimate his USG%.
